docs.title: Anthropic isn’t the end of man
docs.text:
Global 
 Anthropic isn’t the end of man
 Holman W. Jenkins , The Wall Street Journal 3 min read 28 Oct 2026, 02:54 PM IST 
 Summary
 Its prospectus says more about national security than it does human extinction. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The world is rightly aflutter this week over the “PHP” vulnerability, one of many cyber bugs exposed by AI that the world’s cyberwarriors are desperately trying to fix one step ahead of the world’s hackers. But notice this is already different from the science-fiction fears birthed before AI was a real thing, when simple premises permitted so many startling conclusions.
 Remember when artificial superintelligence would outsmart every human effort to control it, because, see, it would be superintelligent? There would be “foom”—it would explode on the world overnight and have us under its thumb before we knew it. This would happen when AI starts training AI, known as “recursive self-improvement.”
 But then reality happens. Fears that once seemed realistic stop seeming realistic. AI companies, it turns out, don’t start an automated training process and come back later to see what it hatched. Any fooming process would quickly be self-liquidating, exhausting its supply of chips and power.
 OpenAI CEO Sam Altman perhaps doesn’t control the human future after all since he doesn’t even control his own company, owning zero percent of the stock. Or its flagship chatbot, which will happily tell you Mr. Altman is “increasingly questioned as a trustworthy steward of a technology that could reshape society.”
 Now comes the most awaited stock offering of the AI era. Missing the point, Bloomberg headlines its story: “Anthropic Flags ‘Existential Risks’ in Long-Awaited IPO Filing.”
 Uh huh. Put it this way. Buying the stock, you might lose money. But if extinction is humanity’s fate, not buying it won’t save you.
 Happily, real-world facts are starting to influence the story arc. Martin Peers of The Information points out that “Anthropic’s ability to even release its best models is diminishing” due to government intervention.
 “After Mythos”—the ultra-cyber-capable model Anthropic felt obliged to withhold from the market in April—“the whole world changed in D.C.,” says anti-AI organizer Connor Leahy.
 Aleksander Madry, an MIT professor, unexpectedly returned to a recently abandoned job at OpenAI to participate in what he calls a “different regime of AI progress” centered on safety and security challenges.
 The real gist of Anthropic’s warning to investors? They are entering terra incognita in how society will treat and regulate this new technology—though don’t worry, those who warned of human extinction will soon be saying “I told you so” when AI mistakenly deletes your email.
 Electricity, to which AI is often compared, came into the world before the last century’s giant expansion of government and the national-security state. More significantly, AI landed at a moment when cyber was a mission-critical focus of the U.S. defense and national intelligence establishment. That’s practically all you need to know. The extent of this importance is hard to exaggerate—from monitoring the world’s vast and growing data flows to protecting the data and infrastructure on which the fully digitized U.S. economy now relies.
 Anthropic’s prospectus mentions “existential risks to humanity” three times. It mentions national security 22 times. If coming models are as powerful as their antics in the lab indicate, their availability to the public, if any, will be strictly controlled by Washington. If you have doubts, look at the stock market. No obvious end-of-the-world trade is happening, but shares of cybersecurity companies have been straight up since Mythos was unveiled.
 This week economist and longtime AI cheerleader Tyler Cowen conceded the obvious to the New York Times. The prevailing political dynamic “puts more weight on our national-security establishment and the Defense Department. I don’t feel entirely comfortable with that, but I think that’s what it’s going to have to be.”
 Yep. Don’t expect to get your hands on the kind of ultra-sophisticated tools that will be available only to Anthropic’s “trusted-access” partners—i.e., those approved by government. The midwifing of advanced AI into the world economy will increasingly be controlled by two bureaucracies, ours and China’s.
 But a separate phenomenon remains the availability of increasingly sophisticated chatbots, acting as adviser rather than agent. These are less likely to be inhibited by government, partly for First Amendment reasons in the U.S. This might be a bigger revolution than we appreciate.
 Why? Humans are highly social apes with big brains—and these things have eternally been in tension. You might have learned as much from the allegory of the emperor’s new clothes or the discoveries of behavioral economics. The progress may not be dramatic. It might even be subliminal. But a large and unexplored scope exists for improving society’s collective thinking processes. We obviously need help. That help could be arriving just as democracy confronts daunting demographic, fiscal, national-security and—yes—technological challenges.

docs.title: Attractive interest rates, fee waivers: What to watch for in festive loan offers
docs.text:
Mint Money 
 Attractive interest rates, fee waivers: What to watch for in festive loan offers
 Ananya Grover 9 min read 28 Oct 2026, 03:12 PM IST 
 Summary
 The real benefit depends on the borrower's credit profile, the lender's eligibility criteria and the hidden charges. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Diwali is considered one of the most auspicious times for big-ticket purchases, whether it is buying a home or a vehicle. To tap into this festive sentiment, banks are rolling out loan offers, such as interest-rate concessions and processing-fee waivers.
 These discounts may appeal more given that the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) increased the repo rate by 25 basis points on 7 October and is now moving towards recalibrated tightening.
 Santosh Agarwal, chief executive of consumer credit and financial services marketplace Paisabazaar, said that lenders have traditionally focused on making offers more attractive during the festive season by offering lower interest rates for a limited period or waiver of processing fees.
 But, given the broad macro factors, including the rate hike, festive discounts need closer scrutiny, as this year they may not make loans as lucrative as earlier. Mint looks at some of the offers:
 Home loans
 For new homebuyers, Jagadeesh Mohan, co-founder of EMI Saver, said banks offer festive concessions to meet loan volume and profitability targets, while developers time launches to coincide with the auspicious homebuying season.
 Most home loans in India carry floating interest rates linked to an external benchmark, such as RBI’s repo rate. The lending rate comprises the benchmark rate, a spread that usually remains fixed for a period, and any borrower-specific concessions based on their credit profile.
 Mohan said that, of the 25-basis-point rate hike, most banks have absorbed only 5-10bps as part of their festive campaigns through a combination of spread compression and enhanced borrower concessions, meaning their effective lending rates for new customers have risen by only 20bps.
 For example, Bank of Baroda had increased the rate after the RBI repo rate hike announcement, but has now lowered it by 5bps effective 10 October, Mangesh Zope, founder of Peaceful Loans, said.
 The bank said, in response to Mint 's emailed questions, that as part of its festive campaign, its home-loan interest rates start from 7.40% per annum, with quick sanctions and a complete waiver of processing fees until 31 October. It also offers an additional interest-rate discount of 5bps to women and 10bps to certain other eligible borrowers, including people under 40, employees who receive their salaries through BoB accounts, and qualifying high-net-worth individuals and Baroda Radiance customers.
 State Bank of India ( SBI ) and IDBI Bank are also advertising concessional rates, but, according to experts, these are reserved for borrowers with excellent credit scores of 800 and above. Banks follow risk-based pricing, so the final rate can depend on your credit profile and other factors, including your employer or your relationship with the bank.
 While short-term discount windows can help lock in a lower spread, various banks’ terms state that the spread is subject to change at the bank’s discretion or if the borrower’s credit profile deteriorates. Also, check whether concessions depend on signing up for add-ons like property insurance, and whether you really need them.
 Pankaj Mathpal, founder and managing director of Optima Money, said while borrowers should take advantage of the offers, they should not take a loan simply because concessions are there.
 He added that borrowers should assess their long-term repayment capacity rather than relying on the loan amount or EMI a bank says they are eligible for, and consider other charges associated with the loan.
 Processing fee waivers
 And it’s not just a discount on the interest rates, some banks are also advertising waivers or discounts on processing fees that cover the bank's internal costs to verify your profile and approve the loan and typically range from 0.25% to 2% of the total loan amount (plus 18% goods and services tax), though some lenders cap it at a fixed minimum or maximum amount.
 Zope said that in an affordable housing loan, a processing fee waiver is meaningful as a festive offer, but big-ticket home-loan borrowers actively seek banks that will refund the processing fee fully or partially, or agents who offer cashback on processing fees regardless of the festive season.
 A loan offer with a processing fee waiver can reduce the initial expense, but another with even a slightly lower interest rate can cost you less over the long term, Agarwal said, adding that borrowers should compare multiple options on all parameters, including the APR (annual percentage rate) or the total yearly cost.
 Vehicle and personal loans
 Vehicle and personal loans are also advertised at attractive rates. Opinion 
 Godzilla El Niño: India must do all it can to prepare rural India for it
 Mint Editorial Board 3 min read 29 Oct 2026, 07:30 AM IST 
 Summary
 The government should work with states to chalk out a drought management and relief plan as this weather phenomenon gets worse. It is set to not only stokes prices but also hurt rural incomes. Here some measures policymakers should consider taking. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The El Niño in the Pacific is literally off-the-charts and may gain “unprecedented” strength by December, the World Meteorological Organization warned in an update last week. It simply means the world is entering uncharted territory. By now, it’s almost certain that the 2026-27 El Niño will be the strongest ever, surpassing past extreme weather events seen in 2015-16, and way back in 1877-78 when millions perished in India and China. 
 The ongoing El Niño’s first casualty was the south-west monsoon, which recorded a deficit of 13%, the widest since 2015. 
 The impacts are already being felt in crops such as rice, sugarcane, maize and pulses. Prices of these crops are already rising. A bigger worry is the impact this ‘Godzilla’ El Niño may have on the winter crop season beginning next month. A warmer winter and early onset of a hottest-ever summer in 2027 can singe the wheat crop. 
 As the El Niño peaks by December, parts of India may see crippling water shortages by February-March next year, or even earlier. Cities such as Hyderabad, Mumbai and Pune are already witnessing water shortages. Both the crop and non-crop farm sector (including livestock, dairy and poultry) could be hit hard as feed, fodder and water shortages intensify. 
 Agricultural economist and former Niti Aayog member Ramesh Chand has warned that farm sector growth may be close to zero or even turn negative in 2026-27. The agricultural growth rate was already losing steam, with growth at 3% in 2025-26, compared to 4.2% in the year-ago period. 
 Farm and non-farm wage growth have also been sluggish over the past year, as Mint columnist Himanshu pointed out recently. Real (inflation-adjusted) farm wages fell by 1.9% in August compared to the year-ago period while non-farm wages declined 2.1% over the same period, his estimates show. 
 This means that rural incomes are already stressed, and the super El Niño would add to that stress. 
 A small farmer in India is also a consumer purchasing multiple food items from the market. She is also a day wage earner. So, as food inflation increases, families in rural India will be pushed to spend more on essentials, impacting discretionary spending on fast moving consumer goods as well as durables. Rural demand is likely to be hit hard. 
 At a time of rising bond yields and fiscal stress, it is important for the Union government to set aside adequate funds for rural relief in the coming months. 
 One may recall that the state of Maharashtra was the first to launch a rural employment guarantee scheme following a crippling drought in 1972. It inspired the National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme in 2005. Funds for the revamped version of that scheme—the Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin)—should be hiked to help ease rural distress. 
 The rural development ministry should ensure that enough person-days of work are generated and that families work for the full 125 days promised under the scheme. Insurance companies should be nudged to hasten crop damage assessments and pay-outs. 
 Karnataka, Maharashtra and Telangana have already announced a drought. The Union government should work with states to chalk out a drought management and relief plan. From water to wages, there’s a lot to fix in the coming months.

 Going global: Step-by-step guide to buying international stocks
 Ann Jacob 5 min read 28 Oct 2026, 10:10 AM IST 
 Summary
 Indian investors can access US stocks through regulated platforms, but forex charges, brokerage, tax rules and disclosure requirements can add to the cost. Here’s what to know before investing. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Investing in foreign markets like the US allows Indian investors to diversify beyond domestic equities and gain exposure to global stocks. Indians can use various regulatory channels to access international stocks. Here’s a breakdown of how one can get started, how insurance works, what charges apply, brokerage charges, and taxation.
 Getting started 
 Indian residents can invest abroad under the Reserve Bank of India’s Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), which allows individuals to remit up to $250,000 per financial year for foreign stocks, overseas-listed exchange-traded funds (ETFs) and other permitted purposes, including travel and education.
 To facilitate investing, Indian platforms operate through regulated frameworks. "In August 2025, IFSCA (the regulator for GIFT City) introduced the Global Access Provider (GAP) framework, a regulated channel for Indians to invest in international markets," explained Puneet Maheshwari, director at Upstox.
 Platforms such as Upstox and Groww hold GAP licences through their GIFT City entities, alongside direct LRS routes. "The platform acts as the regulated gateway, while accounts are opened in the customer's name with a US broker partner regulated by the SEC and FINRA," noted a Groww spokesperson. Viram Shah, co-founder and CEO of Vested Finance, added that investors can buy listed foreign securities or overseas funds under these rules.
 Remittance costs 
 Once the account is set up, investors transfer rupees, which are converted into foreign currency and remitted abroad.
 "Direct bank transfers can be expensive, with FX conversion fees ranging between 1.5% and 2%," noted Shah. "However, platform partnerships with banks help lower FX rates to between 0.5% and 1.5% without the fixed transaction fees."
 Tax collected at source (TCS) applies to LRS remittances exceeding ₹ 10 lakh per financial year. "There is no TCS up to ₹ 10 lakh annually. Above that, TCS is 20%, which can be claimed back or adjusted in your income tax return," said Maheshwari.
 Custody and protection
 Investors can buy shares, including fractional shares for as little as $1, according to the platforms. However, Shah cautions that under LRS rules, investors cannot keep cash idle in trading accounts for more than one year.
 Shares are held electronically in the US depository system, with investors recorded as beneficial owners. "Each investor's account is opened in their own name with the US broker partner," confirmed the Groww spokesperson.
 "Accounts are covered by the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC) up to $500,000, including up to $250,000 in cash, if the US broker fails," explained Maheshwari. Shah added that SIPC protection mirrors US citizen coverage but does not protect against stock price declines.
 Brokerage and forex
 Costs vary across platforms and can include brokerage, foreign exchange mark-ups and statutory charges. Upstox charges 0.25% per trade, capped at $25. Groww charges 0.1% or $1 per executed order. Zerodha charges 0.10% of the trade value per order, with a minimum of $0.01 and a maximum of $10 for buying and selling US stocks and ETFs , according to its website.
 Forex charges also vary. Upstox's partner-bank conversion typically ranges from 1% to 3.5%, depending on the service provider and transaction type. Zerodha charges a currency-conversion mark-up of 0.4-1.4% above the RBI reference rate, according to its website.
 Financial services company Interactive Brokers offers fixed or tiered brokerage. Investors should compare these charges with forex costs and expected trading frequency to identify the most cost-efficient option for their portfolio.
 When it comes to taxes, investors need to note that US dividends face a 25% tax deducted at source for Indian residents filing the W-8BEN form, which can be claimed as a Foreign Tax Credit (FTC) by filing Form 67 in India. Because dividends are taxed at applicable income tax slab rates in India, investors in the 30% tax bracket must pay the remaining 5% tax locally after claiming the 25% FTC.
 Capital gains are taxed under Indian domestic tax rules. Foreign equities have a 24-month holding-period threshold for long-term capital gains (LTCG), compared with 12 months for domestic listed equities. Short-term capital gains (STCG) on holdings of 24 months or less are taxed at applicable slab rates, while LTCG on holdings exceeding 24 months is taxed at 12.5%.
 Investors must also disclose foreign assets, bank accounts and trading accounts in Schedule FA of their income-tax return (ITR-2 or ITR-3) every year, even if they earned no dividends or capital gains during the financial year.
 Choose carefully
 Pankaj Mathpal, founder of Optima Money Managers, recommends that investors consider international exposure but start with funds rather than individual stocks.
 "It would be better to invest through a mutual fund or ETF route. For the mutual fund route, most AMCs are not accepting fresh subscriptions as their limits have already been exhausted, so the international ETF route can be explored. If you want to invest in large names like Amazon, Tesla, or Nvidia, investing in broad indices like the Nasdaq 100 or S&P 500 offers better diversification," said Mathpal.
 Many international ETFs listed on domestic exchanges currently trade at premiums to their net asset value (NAV) because domestic fund houses cannot create fresh units after exhausting their RBI overseas investment limits.
 "For direct international stocks, people who have good knowle

News CDSCO drug alert: Himachal pulls 92 substandard batches, halts 96 pharma units Priyanka Sharma 3 min read 28 Oct 2026, 05:43 PM IST Summary State health authorities ask patients to stop using flagged batches as 70 drug samples produced in the state fail critical ingredient tests while 22 show minor defects. Gift this article Check your portfolio This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you. Subscribe to enjoy similar stories. Subscribe now New Delhi: The Himachal Pradesh Drugs Control Administration has asked patients and the public to stop using specific batches of medicines declared ‘not of standard quality’ (NSQ) by the central drug regulator, according to the two senior government officials familiar with the matter and documents reviewed by Mint . The alert follows the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's (CDSCO) September 2026 report, which flagged 330 drug samples nationwide as sub-standard. Of these, 92 originated from Himachal Pradesh manufacturers. State health authorities confirmed that 70 of the 92 failed critical efficacy parameters—specifically assay and dissolution tests—while 22 showed minor defects, such as labelling issues. To enforce compliance, the state has ordered 96 pharmaceutical facilities to halt manufacturing, either entirely or across specific sections, pending corrective actions. The state accounts for roughly a third of India's domestic drug supplies alongside large export volumes. Himachal Pradesh is home to over 650 pharmaceutical manufacturing units, largely based in Baddi. About 70% of these are micro, small and medium enterprises ( MSMEs ) and 15-20% are large companies. The state accounts for about 35% of India's total domestic drug formulations, meaning every third drug on a chemist's shelf in India originates from Himachal Pradesh. Widely prescribed medicines flagged According to the CDSCO’s website, several widely prescribed medicines manufactured across Solan and Baddi in Himachal Pradesh were declared NSQ after failing critical active ingredient tests: Aspo Pharmaceuticals’ Namik-MR tablets , indicated for muscle pain or spasms failed in its aceclofenac content. Multiple respiratory formulations were also flagged, including Pharma Roots Healthcare’s AX Cold syrup , prescribed for allergic cough and congestion, which failed ambroxol hydrochloride levels. Similarly, Alventa Pharma’s Healtuss LS and Ultra Drugs Formulations’ Cufcott LS , both bronchodilator and expectorant syrups indicated for productive cough and asthma-related airway congestion, failed tests for ambroxol hydrochloride and levosalbutamol. Saar Biotech’s K-Coff-D syrup , used to treat dry cough, nasal blockage, and allergic cold symptoms, was cited for deficient phenylephrine hydrochloride content. In the topical analgesic category, Cent Cure’s Gone Gel , applied for joint pain, musculoskeletal aches, and sprains, failed the required standard for methyl salicylate. State cites high volumes “The volume of substandard samples must be evaluated in proportion to the state’s massive manufacturing output. Himachal Pradesh contributes to approximately one-third of domestic supplies, besides exporting big volumes of drug formulations,” Himachal Pradesh health secretary Ashish Singhmar said, pointing out that the state’s share of failed samples actually declined from 34% in July to 28% in September. State drug controller Dr. Manish Kapoor said, “The drugs control administration, Himachal Pradesh, maintains a zero-tolerance approach towards the manufacture or distribution of substandard medicines and every effort is being made to ensure strict compliance of regulatory requirements. F ollowing procedures laid down under the law, not only are the licences to manufacture drug formulations suspended/cancelled by the DCA HP, but at parallel, legal action(s) are also taken by the jurisdictions from where samples get drawn for the purpose of analysis/testing.” “The enforcement is an ongoing administrative check-and-balance: these 96 actions particularly are not entirely on the latest NSQ list. It is an ongoing process where facilities are halted either due to NSQs or when other deficiencies are found during inspections. Increased detection is a positive indicator that our regulatory mechanism is strengthening," he added. Dr. Kapoor also pointed out that drugs often degrade after leaving factories. "There are multiple stress factors in the distribution chain—storage conditions, temperature, humidity, and rough transport—that can cause quality failure. We cannot exclusively blame only manufacturers ." Queries sent to the health ministry and the Drugs Controller General of India on Tuesday remained unanswered at the time of publishing. Queries sent to Aspo Pharmaceuticals, Alventa Pharma, Ultra Drugs, also remained unanswered, while Pharma Roots Healthcare couldn't be contacted.  The winners and losers of Trumponomics
 The Economist 4 min read 27 Oct 2026, 09:02 PM IST 
 Summary
 America’s economy is indeed growing briskly, with output on course to expand at an annualised rate of around 3% in the third quarter. But many of those Mr Trump claimed he would help have lost out, while richer Americans have gained. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 ALL POPULISTS promise much to the working man, but Donald Trump predicted a golden age. Just before the election in 2024, he told voters they were days away from “the best jobs, the biggest paychecks, and the brightest economic future the world has ever seen”. His unorthodox blend of tariffs, tax cuts and deportations, he claimed, would bring down living costs, revive America’s industrial heartland and restore middle-class prosperity.
 Has the president delivered? On October 22nd the White House claimed his policies were driving up wages and fuelling a “blue-collar BOOM”. America’s economy is indeed growing briskly, with output on course to expand at an annualised rate of around 3% in the third quarter. But many of those Mr Trump claimed he would help have lost out, while richer Americans have gained.
 The most politically toxic policies are those that have raised daily costs. The president’s sweeping tariffs have pushed up the cost of consumer goods by roughly 2%, according to the New York Fed. The Budget Lab at Yale estimates they will cost the average household $1,100 this year. The war in Iran has also sent oil prices soaring, and is set to add another $1,000 to the average household’s costs by year’s end.
 Pushing in the other direction, Mr Trump’s flagship tax-and-spending law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, has boosted tax refunds by around $340 on average. The law also created “Trump accounts”, an effort to broaden ownership in the stock market, with eligible newborns entitled to $1,000 to invest in shares. But the law’s biggest gains went to richer Americans, through lower taxes, even as it tightened access to food stamps—with more than 5m Americans losing benefits so far—and to Medicaid, the health-care programme for the poor.
 To tally the net effects of these gains and losses, The Economist combined estimates of the impact of tariffs, higher petrol prices and Mr Trump’s tax-and-spending law across income groups in 2026. We estimate that Mr Trump’s policies will cost the poorest tenth of American households, with average income after taxes and transfers of around $37,000, almost 3% of their income. The richest tenth, with average after-tax incomes of nearly $500,000, will gain nearly 3% (see chart 1). Households in the middle, with average income of roughly $100,000, lose more than $400. That does not account for the effect of a decision, taken by Congressional Republicans last year and endorsed by Mr Trump, to let enhanced Obamacare subsidies expire. That has raised average premiums for individual insurance purchased on exchanges by nearly $800 a year, according to KFF, a health-policy research group.
 Housing costs pose another problem for the president. Mortgage rates, pushed up in part by the inflationary effects of his war in Iran, have climbed above 7%, prompting existing owners to stay put. Adding new supply has become more costly. Last year builders estimated that tariffs on materials would add nearly $11,000 to the cost of a typical new home. His immigration crackdown is fuelling labour shortages, too; in September a survey from the National Association of Home Builders reported that labour costs were up by 4.2% from a year earlier. It is lower-income and middle-class voters, again, who are most pinched. In May sales of starter homes fell by 5.4% from a year earlier, even as luxury-home sales rose by 6.2%, according to Zillow, an online property firm.
 When it comes to jobs, health care and social assistance have accounted for almost all private-sector gains since January 2025, to meet demand from America’s ageing population. The artificial-intelligence boom has been another bright spot, with data-centre investment creating roughly 180,000 new jobs in industries related to the build-out. In other sectors, though, private employment has barely budged. Annual wage growth across the private sector has slowed from 4% to 3%; rising inflation means that workers’ hourly pay is 0.7% lower in real terms than a year ago. Labour’s share of nonfarm business output has fallen to its lowest level since records began in 1947 (technical changes to how business owners’ earnings are classified explain only some of the decline).
 A renaissance in manufacturing jobs has been particularly elusive. Though manufacturing output has risen, manufacturing employment has fallen by some 20,000 since January 2025, while factory workers’ wages have failed to keep pace with inflation over the past year. In North Carolina, which Mr Trump won in 2024 and which now looks set to elect a Democrat to the Senate, nearly 9,000 factory jobs have disappeared over the past year.
 Americans invested in the stock market have more to celebrate, as the AI bonanza has driven up the value of the S&P 500. But the impact is, once again, lopsided. Of the $17trn increase in Americans’ equity and mutual-fund wealth since the end of 2024, nearly 90% accrued to the richest tenth of households, compared with just 0.6% for the poorer half, according to data from the Federal Reserve (see chart 2).
 These phenomena have not gone unnoticed. Nearly two-thirds of Americans think that Mr Trump’s economic policies have made conditions worse, according to a recent survey by the Pew Research Centre; the same is true of 35% of Republicans and Republican-leaning independents, nearly twice the share in January. Voters who are particularly affected by rising fuel costs and tariffs, such as farmers, are tilting towards Democrats. Mr Trump is now promising $5,0

 American bosses are desperately trying to de-MAGAfy
 The Economist 1 min read 27 Oct 2026, 08:53 PM IST 
 Summary
 Many bosses have abandoned that even-handedness over the past two years. Companies identified a window of opportunity to advance their agendas. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 American bosses once acted on the knowledge that, in politics, the wheel always turns. Parties came in and out of power, and so companies curried favour with both Republicans and Democrats regardless of who controlled the White House or Capitol Hill.
 Many bosses have abandoned that even-handedness over the past two years. Companies identified a window of opportunity to advance their agendas, says Reggie Babin of Akin, a lobbying shop. Since Donald Trump’s return to power, pushing through long-desired mergers or securing regulatory changes has often meant abandoning bipartisanship—and dignity, judging by the many corporate donations to Mr Trump’s garish new ballroom.
 In a few days, however, the president is predicted to emerge from the midterm elections with a far weaker grip on Washington. Accordingly, much of corporate America has been desperately trying to scrub off its spray tan and deflate its lip filler. But rebuilding ties with the Democrats will not be easy.
 One way this shows up is in the people businesses appoint to handle government relations. In January 2025, the same month Mr Trump was inaugurated, Meta elevated Joel Kaplan, its longtime Republican-whisperer, to be the social-media giant’s chief emissary. On October 20th it announced that Mr Kaplan will be leaving the company. Paramount Skydance, which recently completed its takeover of Warner Bros Discovery with the president’s blessing, has hired a former staffer from the Biden administration to help court the Democrats. Other companies that have enlisted former Democratic aides in the past six months include Palantir, a maker of data-analysis tools, as well as Polymarket and Kalshi, two prediction markets.
 The tilt away from Mr Trump can also be seen in America Inc’s donations. Companies are barred from giving candidates money from their own coffers. But they can co-ordinate donations by setting up political action committees (PACs), which solicit voluntary contributions, mostly from company executives. Those executives can also give to candidates directly or through trusts.
 The Economist examined federal filings covering donations by business leaders and their families across these channels. In the second quarter of 2026, the latest period for which data are available in full, 33% of their giving went to Democrats, up slightly from 31% across 2025. Yet that vastly understates the shift, as a disproportionate share of mega-donors support Republicans. Strip out the ten biggest—including Elon Musk—and 51% of donations in the second quarter went to the Democrats, up from 36% throughout last year.
 For the most part, America Inc still draws the line at supporting socialists. Of the $287m that executives donated to Democrats in the first half of this year, a mere $9m has gone to progressives, including those endorsed by the Democratic Socialists of America. Take out the donations given by Saikat Chakrabarti, most of which went to the entrepreneur’s own unsuccessful primary bid, and the figure drops to just over $4m.
 America’s bosses, however, may find that even moderate Democrats have become unreceptive to their overtures. Stopping data centres is not the only anti-corporate rallying cry that has pervaded the midterms. In Iowa, big agriculture is the villain; in Alaska, it is big fish. One former Democratic official sums up the party’s new outlook on corporate America bluntly: “We demand blood.”
 In Silicon Valley the nervousness is palpable. Chris Hughes, a co-founder of Facebook and friend of the Democrats, notes that many tech bosses spent much of the past two years “running around Washington” trying to shape regulation in their interests. One venture capitalist predicts “a reckoning” after the midterms for those who cosied up to Mr Trump. “History is not going to look back particularly favourably on those who leaned in.”
 Sensing the threat, some have gone on the attack. Consider the contest for a Senate seat in Ohio. Sherrod Brown, the Democratic candidate seeking to return to the Senate, is a vocal critic of the crypto industry. Fairshake, its flagship PAC network, is thus spending $55m in a bid to prevent his comeback. But some prominent industry figures—including Chris Larsen, co-founder of Ripple, a crypto-infrastructure provider—have opposed the effort, worrying that it will create animosity with Democratic lawmakers, and that Mr Brown is unlikely to forget the attacks if he wins. Mr Larsen has donated through other channels to the Democrat’s campaign.
 Capitol punishment
 The blue wave may end up smaller than polls suggest. But even if the Democrats take the House only narrowly and lose the Senate, they will be able to give businesses a headache. Control of the lower chamber would give Democratic committee chairs the power to subpoena company files and call executives to testify. That could cause embarrassment, or worse.
 Washington lawyers say they have been fielding calls since the start of this year about potential investigations. In some cases, they have already been hired to parse employees’ actions and communications for indiscretions that could become public, and have been working to pick and train telegenic witnesses from their clients’ ranks. Edward O’Callaghan of Cahill, one law firm, says he has been counselling some businesses to pre-emptively meet influential members of Congress in a bid to avoid public hearings. Where Democratic support seems unlikely, they can instead prepare Republicans with favourable information to use in a hearing.

docs.title: TVS family feud: Venu Srinivasan, son and wife along with daughter file caveats
docs.text:
News 
 TVS family feud: Venu Srinivasan, son and wife along with daughter file caveats
 Varun Sood , Satish John 5 min read 28 Oct 2026, 05:40 AM IST 
 Summary
 TVS Motor Co. chairman-emeritus Venu Srinivasan, son Sudarshan Venu, wife Mallika Srinivasan, and daughter Lakshmi Venu have filed a total of eight caveats in two Chennai courts 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The feuding family members of the TVS Group have filed a slew of caveats in Chennai courts, as an ownership dispute hangs over the Chennai-based business conglomerate. TVS Motor Co. chairman-emeritus Venu Srinivasan, son Sudarshan Venu, wife Mallika Srinivasan, and daughter Lakshmi Venu have filed a total of eight caveats in two Chennai courts, a Mint review of court records showed.
 On 12 October, Venu Srinivasan filed the first, naming Lakshmi and Mallika Srinivasan in the City Civil Court. The same day, Mallika Srinivasan filed a caveat, naming Venu and Sudarshan. All four family members also filed caveats in the Commercial Court the same day. Lakshmi Venu also filed a caveat in the City Civil Court the next day, naming her father, while Sudarshan filed a case against his sister.
 The caveats ensure that the court hears a party before passing any order over a petition moved by the rival party. In the TVS family dispute, the father and son are ranged on one side, and the mother and daughter on the other.
 The caveats were filed three days after Mint reported on 9 October that Mallika and Lakshmi were seeking "a fair settlement" over the assets of the TVS Group, as patriarch Venu Srinivasan was reported to have given much of the ownership to son Sudarshan Venu.
 “Is this (filing a caveat) a precursor to this ownership dispute going to court? One cannot say for sure,” said an executive who works with Mallika Srinivasan. “Every effort is being made to resolve this amicably. But both sides need to be open to settling,” said the executive, declining to elaborate.
 Emails sent to Venu Srinivasan and Mallika Srinivasan seeking comment went unanswered.
 “As stated earlier in their joint statement, Dr Lakshmi Venu and Mallika Srinivasan reiterate their desire for an amicable resolution through transparent discussions and dialogue,” a spokesperson for the two said.
 Split and after
 The wider TVS business was divided between Venu Srinivasan and his cousins in 2020. Four years later, Venu Srinivasan and his family members signed another family agreement, under which his son, Sudarshan, and daughter, Lakshmi, were given control of two public companies: automaker TVS Motor and die-casting company Sundaram-Clayton Ltd. Under this agreement, Venu Srinivasan and Sudarshan control TVS Holdings, the main holding company of TVS Motor Company. They also control the privately owned financial services and real estate business, according to a Mint review of the 2024 Memorandum of Understanding.
 Srinivasan and Lakshmi control Sundaram-Clayton Ltd, the listed die-casting company. Venu Srinivasan wields control over TVS Motor and Sundaram-Clayton. Mallika and Lakshmi separately control Tractors and Farm Equipment Ltd (TAFE).
 The 2024 family agreement is now facing a challenge—Mallika Srinivasan says it was only about managing the businesses, non-compete clauses and using the brand, and did not split ownership of the businesses among the children, the fourth generation of TV Sundaram Iyengar, the founder of the 115-year-old TVS industrial group.
 “No economic settlement has taken place within the Venu Srinivasan family,” Mallika, chairperson and managing director of Tractors and Farm Equipment Ltd (TAFE), told Mint on 13 October, in her first on-record telephone interview on the dispute. “I do believe that the legitimate economic interests of both children must be recognized fairly and equitably,” she said.
 The dispute comes at a time when Venu Srinivasan wields considerable influence over the Tata Group, the country’s largest conglomerate. His support for Tata Sons chairman N. Chandrasekaran for a third five-year term and his backing to make the Group company public are at the centre of a conflict with most of the Tata Trustees, including chairman Noel Tata.
 Stake tangle
 TVS family members own 59.09% of Sundaram-Clayton. VS Trust, with Venu Srinivasan as sole trustee, owns 46.83%, while a family branch owns 6.87% through TSF Investments Ltd. Srinivasan holds 4.38% personally, and Mallika and Lakshmi own 0.26% and 0.75%.

 Trump moves to weaken methane emissions rules for oil and gas
 Benoît Morenne , The Wall Street Journal 4 min read 28 Oct 2026, 02:51 PM IST 
 Summary
 Small fossil-fuel producers have opposed regulations to curb releases of the potent greenhouse gas. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The Trump administration is moving to dismantle Biden-era rules that sought to limit emissions of methane, a potent greenhouse gas, answering a key demand of some of its oil-and-gas allies.
 President Trump is set to announce the measures at a rally in Lubbock, Texas, on Tuesday, according to an administration official. Rising energy costs have become a major issue ahead of the midterm elections, and the administration has described the planned rollback as a way to lower bills.
 The Environmental Protection Agency is preparing to propose easing regulations for wells that emit large amounts of methane, rescinding a program to identify large methane leaks and allowing fossil-fuel producers to flare more natural gas, among other changes.
 The agency said earlier this month that the regulations “posed a monumental threat” to workers and businesses in the oil-and-gas industry—and caused higher energy prices. It said loosening the regulations would save an estimated $45 billion.
 “The methane rules have been very cumbersome for us,” said Chad McDougall, vice president at JMA Energy, a privately held oil-and-gas producer in Oklahoma City.
 Bloomberg first reported the planned announcement.
 The proposed changes amount to an overhaul of the regulatory edifice the U.S. has built to curb releases in the oil-and-gas industry. It is the largest industrial source of methane emissions in the nation, according to the EPA.
 Scientists and policymakers say reducing leaks of methane—the main component of natural gas—at oil-and-gas wells is crucial to help combat climate change. The gas is 80 times as potent at trapping heat from solar radiation as carbon dioxide over its first 20 years in the atmosphere.
 Large oil-and-gas producers have been supportive of federal methane regulations, in part because they want to keep selling their product to climate-minded buyers abroad. But smaller operators focused on the domestic market have decried the rules as bankruptcy-inducing. They have said compliance costs are prohibitive and would lead to mom-and-pops shutting production.
 One group that pushed for a full repeal was oil billionaire Harold Hamm’s lobby, the Domestic Energy Producers Alliance. It said some of the rules functioned “less like an emission-control standard and more like a production ban on new domestic energy development.” Hamm and his private company, Continental Resources, donated more than $3 million to help Trump get re-elected.
 The Environmental Defense Fund, an environmental nonprofit, said rolling back the regulations would create more methane pollution and health risks for communities living near oil-and-gas operations. It said it would also translate into wasted natural gas that is burned instead of being shipped to markets.
 “At a time when Americans are facing high energy costs, EPA should not give oil-and-gas companies more room to waste a domestic resource,” said Jon Goldstein, associate vice president, energy transition at the Environmental Defense Fund.
 The Biden administration issued the methane rules as part of a broader global effort to contain emissions. They affected thousands of wells, storage tanks and natural-gas processing plants, and required companies to replace leaky, older equipment and buy new monitoring tools. Biden said at the time that the measures would lead to an 87% reduction in U.S. methane emissions from covered sources by 2030 from 2005 levels.
 One major target was the 760,000 wells that produce negligeable amounts of fossil fuels individually. Taken together, they account for over 7.4% of U.S. oil production and about 8.2% of U.S. natural-gas production, according to the National Stripper Well Association.
 The wells produce a disproportionate amount of methane: Studies in recent years have shown that they account for approximately 60% of the U.S. natural-gas production emissions and about 40% of the U.S. oil production emissions.
 Some of the Biden rules aimed at reducing large leaks or releases of methane at oil-and-gas facilities and forcing companies to address them. They allowed third parties to notify the EPA of releases.
 Andrew Logan, a senior director at environmental nonprofit Ceres, said the regulations had a profound impact. Companies anticipated the rules ahead of time and worked to reduce their emissions, which prevented millions of tons of methane from leaking. It allowed companies to sell more natural gas and collect more cash.
 Logan said weakening the rules was unlikely to spur more production and lower energy prices; instead, companies would pocket more profit from the regulatory savings. A separate EPA measure to allow companies to torch more natural gas—as long as they flare efficiently—might damp the appetite for building pipelines to ship the product to markets.
 “It could actually bring down the amount of gas you would have sold,” he said.
 Toby Rice, chief executive of EQT, one of the largest U.S. natural-gas producers, said the industry needs smart regulations. He said that shutting down low-producing wells might help with methane emissions, but that coal, a polluting source of energy, would replace the missing supply.
 “You’d actually be going backwards towards your greenhouse gas emissions objectives.”

 How Bolsonaro fled Brazil: decoys, a private jet and a friend in the White House
 Vera Bergengruen , Samantha Pearson , Ryan Dubé , Philip Wegmann , The Wall Street Journal 7 min read 29 Oct 2026, 06:57 AM IST 
 Summary
 After losing Brazil’s election, Flávio Bolsonaro fled to Miami in an elaborate operation aided by Trump’s inner circle and Argentina’s president, Javier Milei. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 Less than 24 hours after losing Brazil’s presidential election, Flávio Bolsonaro appeared to vanish into a convoy of four dark cars.
 After pulling away from his home in Brasília on Monday evening, the vehicles split in different directions, leaving journalists and authorities scrambling to determine which one carried Bolsonaro. By the next afternoon, the former presidential candidate’s allies were telling reporters he had already reached Florida.
 As Brazilian and international outlets reported that Bolsonaro had left the country, he was still in Brazil, while a private jet waited for him across the border in Argentina. At 12:21 a.m. Wednesday, the Gulfstream G400 took off from Puerto Iguazú and whisked him to Ecuador and then Miami, where his entry was facilitated by Trump allies his family spent years cultivating.
 The getaway—which relied heavily on deception and decoys—sparked a global guessing game that left even some of Bolsonaro’s closest allies in Washington and Brazil in the dark about his whereabouts.
 After Bolsonaro stepped off the plane in Miami on Wednesday morning wearing a navy polo shirt and a backpack, uniformed officers used umbrellas to shield him and his family from cameras. Their arrival followed an extraordinary effort by a small circle of influential Trump allies, senior U.S. officials and Argentine President Javier Milei to help him fly to the U.S. and secure entry, despite a Brazilian court order barring Bolsonaro from leaving the country.
 Referring to himself as the “leader of Brazil,” Bolsonaro thanked President Trump for welcoming him to a “land of freedoms” and Milei for his “courage” and “sense of justice” in a statement from Miami Wednesday.
 After Trump personally approved admitting Bolsonaro and his family to the U.S. on Tuesday, Secretary of State Marco Rubio moved to issue them visas, according to people familiar with the arrangements. But the family entered the country under humanitarian parole, which allows them to remain for one year, the people said.
 The operation to whisk Bolsonaro out of Brazil to the U.S. took shape on Monday, as allies grew concerned that he could face arrest. Although the criminal investigations into Bolsonaro predated the election, the Supreme Court order barring him from leaving Brazil and requiring him to surrender his passports came shortly after his defeat and fueled accusations that President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was determined to punish his political rival.
 Working with Flávio Bolsonaro’s well-connected younger brother Eduardo, a small group including Trump adviser Jason Miller secured a charter jet to take him from Argentina to Florida.
 The Trump administration’s decision to provide refuge to Bolsonaro marks the culmination of the family’s yearslong lobbying campaign to enlist the U.S. president and his inner circle in its legal and political battles at home. The personal alliance between the two most powerful political families in the hemisphere has reshaped relations between the U.S. and Brazil. Last year, Trump imposed steep tariffs on the country citing its treatment of Bolsonaro and sanctioned the same Supreme Court justice who barred Bolsonaro from leaving Brazil.
 President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won an unprecedented fourth term in Brazil. WSJ’s Samantha Pearson explains what Lula’s victory means for President Trump and his right-wing allies in Latin America. Photo: Paulo Lopes/Xinhua/ZUMA Press
 Now, what began as a domestic political and legal battle in Brazil is becoming a test of how far Trump is willing to wield American power on behalf of a foreign political dynasty—with potentially far-reaching consequences for the second-largest democracy in the Americas.
 Bolsonaro intends to set up a political operation in exile from the U.S., people involved in discussions with him said. But with the U.S. midterm elections days away, the White House has given little indication that it intends to go beyond offering Bolsonaro refuge or that Trump will expend political capital challenging da Silva’s re-election victory, despite pressure from allies in Washington, according to two people involved in the discussions.
 Trump declined to comment when reporters asked him about Bolsonaro declaring himself the rightful president of Brazil. “I thought they were treated very unfairly,” he said on Wednesday about the Bolsonaros, who he described as “very fine people” earlier in the day. “But I won’t get involved—it was a very strange election, that’s for sure.”
 Da Silva’s victory in Sunday’s runoff election against Bolsonaro was recognized by more than 50 countries, including Latin American leaders across the political spectrum. He defeated Bolsonaro by more than 4.4 million votes, a margin that international observers said left no doubt about the integrity of the country’s electoral data. Trump, however, has so far refused to formally recognize da Silva’s victory, instead suggesting without evidence that the results might have been rigged.
 The long way to Miami
 On Tuesday, the conservative senator and his family headed to the Argentine border, hundreds of miles away. That night, at 10:50 p.m. local time, Bolsonaro, his wife and their two daughters crossed the Tancredo Neves International Bridge into Puerto Iguazú, Argentina, near where the borders of Brazil, Argentina and Paraguay meet, according to Argentine authorities.
 After crossing the border, Bolsonaro’s vehicle was escorted by Argenti

 US warns Gulf of possible short, intense renewal of Iran war after midterms
 Summer Said , Shelby Holliday , Benoit Faucon , Anat Peled , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 28 Oct 2026, 06:48 AM IST 
 Summary
 There are new signs that the American and Israeli militaries are preparing a potential wave of strikes to muscle Tehran to the negotiating table. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 DUBAI—The U.S. has told several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections, people briefed on the conversations said.
 The communications through diplomatic and military channels are among a growing number of indications that the U.S. and Israel are readying to launch a new round of heavy combat operations against Iran, risking a major escalation in hopes of degrading Tehran’s strength and pushing it toward negotiations.
 The U.S. military is bringing in a Patriot system from Texas to beef up its missile defenses and has moved troops off bases where they were vulnerable in preparation for an escalation, officials familiar with those moves said.
 U.S. forces in the region have been restocking their munitions, and bomber aircraft and jet fighters are preparing for strikes, some of the officials said. An additional aircraft carrier strike group and Marine expeditionary unit are also poised to join an armada of roughly 20 other warships operating in the Middle East next month, although some ships could rotate out.
 President Trump hasn’t decided to go ahead but is leaning toward a large postelection attack that could target Iranian infrastructure and nuclear sites, people familiar with his thinking said.
 The alternative would be to try to cut a deal. Diplomatic efforts by regional mediators continued but had yet to bear fruit.
 “We may do another little Epic Fury,” Trump said at a rally last week, referring to the heavy U.S. and Israeli bombing campaign in the spring. “Or they’ll agree.”
 The White House said it wouldn’t comment on “sensitive military plans that may or may not exist.”
 “President Trump keeps all options on the table to ensure that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon,” the White House said.
 The president has said he won’t attack Iran before the midterms.
 The moves and related planning are meant to give Trump options should he decide to carry out a strike, people familiar with the planning said. The Defense Department said its job is to deliver such options.
 Israel also has prepared plans and targets for a new attack, The Wall Street Journal has reported. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has continued to push for a resumption of strikes in hopes of degrading Iran’s strength and ultimately toppling the regime.
 A return to airstrikes would mean a pivot from the Trump administration’s economic pressure campaign. Tighter sanctions coupled with a naval blockade have cut off Iran’s oil sales for months, shut down much of its air links and cut into overland trade, tightening the squeeze on the country’s already spiraling economy.
 “If there is a need to target a growing threat like missile reconstitution, President Trump should make that case publicly and with as much detail as possible,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the Iran program at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, a U.S. think tank. “⁠Otherwise, at the moment, the U.S. has a winning hand through maintaining sanctions and the blockade. It should stay the course.”
 Many analysts believe Iran isn’t likely to capitulate under further attacks . Iran weathered more than 20,000 strikes by the U.S. and Israel during the most active phase of the war. It nevertheless has continued to attack ships in the Persian Gulf, target U.S. troops and warships, and bring tough demands to the negotiating table.
 “I believe one of the biggest mistakes Israel and the United States continue to make is assuming that another round of strikes against Iran, including attacks on critical infrastructure or the elimination of senior officials, could somehow bring down the regime,” said Danny Citrinowicz, a former Israeli military intelligence official.
 Further bombing could cause the regime to further dig in and become more committed to its missile and nuclear programs, he said.
 WSJ’s Shelby Holliday goes onboard the USS George Washington as it operates in the Arabian Sea, conducting missions in the U.S. war against Iran. Photo: Eve Hartley
 The U.S. and Israel destroyed much of Iran’s nuclear program in the shorter conflict of June 2025.
 Rafael Grossi, head of the International Atomic Energy Agency, told the United Nations Security Council on Tuesday that his agency hasn’t identified any activity to repair or reconstruct any of the facilities damaged by attacks in either of the two wars.
 But he said his inspectors haven’t had access to the facilities to check and said the IAEA hasn’t been able to verify that Iran hasn’t diverted nuclear material. The U.S. has pushed Iran to allow inspectors to return, but it has resisted.
 One of the remaining sites that has raised concern—Pickaxe Mountain—sits under hundreds of feet of rock.
 Trump could use a fresh round of strikes to declare victory and then reduce America’s involvement in the war, even if those strikes don’t deliver a decisive blow, said Seth Jones, a defense and security analyst at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
 “I don’t think anything is going to permanently set back their program,” Jones said of Iran’s nuclear work, but strikes would allow Trump to “start to walk away and say that you had again set back Iran’s nuclear program this time.”

docs.title: 5 start-up lessons from Zero to One by Peter Thiel and Blake Masters: Follow the Money, Mechanics of Mafia and more
docs.text:
A few successful businesses can produce returns much larger than those of others combined. Founders Fund’s Facebook investment clearly showed this pattern. It returned more than all the fund’s other investments together. Thiel advises investors to choose companies capable of returning an entire fund. For founders, the message is about focus. You cannot manage several companies or careers together. Choose something that could matter, then give it your full effort. Great businesses often start with an important discovery others have missed. Peter Thiel calls this a secret: something difficult but possible to uncover. Some secrets concern nature while others concern people. Airbnb, Lyft and Uber recognised unused supply and unmet demand. Their opportunities existed where others saw little value. Fear of risk and satisfaction with existing conditions can prevent such discoveries. Thiel believes mistakes made at the beginning can become impossible to repair. Choosing a co-founder for your start-up , therefore, needs serious thought. Founders should know each other before building a business together. He recommends small boards, ideally with three members. Team members should work full-time. He favours ownership rewards over cash payments. His suggested salary limit for an early-stage CEO is $150,000 annually. For Thiel, a company does not merely have a culture. The company itself is a culture, built around a shared mission. His early PayPal colleagues later built several major businesses. These included LinkedIn, YouTube, Yelp and Palantir. He valued people who enjoyed working together, beyond impressive qualifications. Founders should explain why employees should join, without relying on attractive perks. Assigning each person a single clear job can reduce internal disagreements. Building a product does not automatically bring customers . Businesses must also find an effective way to reach buyers. The money earned from customers must exceed the cost of attracting them. Expensive deals need detailed sales efforts. Cheaper products may depend on advertising or customers spreading the word. Thiel argues that one successful channel can support a great business. Published in 2014, the book includes examples and valuations from an earlier period. Treat its lessons as questions worth careful consideration, rather than as fixed rules. docs.title: Bad press aside, do Bollywood’s plagiarism rows have an on-ground impact?
docs.text:
News 
 Bad press aside, do Bollywood’s plagiarism rows have an on-ground impact?
 Lata Jha 4 min read 28 Oct 2026, 10:33 AM IST 
 Summary
 Lawyers say copyright protects the expression of an idea, not the idea itself. It must be shown that the other side had access to a work and then copied its substance, not merely that two films share a premise 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 New Delhi: The Screenwriters Association has cleared actor Sayani Gupta of alleged copyright infringement in her directorial debut short film Aasmani . Filmmaker Vinita Negi claimed Gupta had borrowed scenes from her unfinished documentary. One consequence: Gupta’s film was withdrawn from the Indian Film Festival of New Zealand in August. 
 Experts say plagiarism rows are a complicated deal in the movie business. To claim that a work has been plagiarized, the claimant must provide evidence of substantial similarity, including early drafts of the script, minutes of meetings in case the script was discussed, and records to establish that the claimant was the first to publish. 
 On the other hand, the commercial consequences of a dispute can arise long before a court decides who is right. A festival opportunity may be affected, a distributor may take a cautious view, or a filmmaker may have to deal with reputational consequences. “Plagiarism” is the commonly used term, but legally, the real question is whether the allegation amounts to copyright infringement .
 “Copyright protects the expression of an idea, not the idea itself. So simply saying ‘someone stole my idea’ is not enough and the person alleging it must prove before court, on evidence, what was actually copied,” said Aishwarya Kaushiq, partner at BTG Advaya, a law firm. 
 If a detailed script or a treatment or concept note was shared in confidence and then misused, there may be a separate breach-of-confidence claim, Kaushiq added. From there, a creator alleging plagiarism can take the civil suit route, usually seeking an injunction and damages, or, in serious cases of knowing copyright infringement, pursue criminal action under the Copyright Act. 
 According to Neeha Nagpal, founding and managing partner at N & Company Legal, the hard part isn’t finding a forum—it’s the law itself. It has to be shown that the other side had access to a work and then copied its substance, not merely that two films share a premise. 
 Breach of confidence 
 “When the work is unpublished or still in progress, proving priority becomes genuinely difficult, which is why writers often pair the copyright claim with a ‘breach of confidence’ argument, saying, ‘I shared this with you in confidence and you used it,’” said Nagpal. “That second limb frequently does the real work.” 
 The uncomfortable truth is that the damage is usually done long before any court says a word. A single allegation—true or not—can get a film pulled from a festival line-up, push back a release, or make a platform go cold on a deal. None of that waits for adjudication. The social-media dimension makes it worse. Once statements of support and signature campaigns start circulating, the reputational hit tends to outlive the vindication. 
 “It (the impact) can be significant, particularly for a short or independent film. A festival selection can bring visibility, reviews, further festival opportunities, distribution conversations and professional recognition,” said Vishal Gehrana, a partner-designate at Karanjawala & Co. “So, the practical consequences of a dispute can sometimes be substantial even before the underlying legal issue is finally decided.” 
 He added that it is important not to confuse a commercial consequence with a legal finding. If a festival decides not to screen a film because of a copyright allegation, that does not by itself establish that copyright has been infringed. It is a decision taken in the face of an allegation. 
 “In the film industry in particular, the commercial clock often moves much faster than the court clock. That is why these disputes have to be approached carefully on both sides, with urgency where protection is genuinely required, but also with sufficient regard for the evidence and for the fact that an allegation is not the same thing as an adjudicated finding,” he said.
 Documentation, registration 
 Much work is required on this front, according to experts. Film producer and distributor Yusuf Shaikh, also founder of low-cost theatre chain Janta Cinema, said many in the movie business are casual about paperwork and timelines. 
 Writers’ bodies in markets like the US are far more transparent. According to Germaine Pereira, a partner at Solomon & Co, a law firm based in Mumbai, it is recommended that the work or script be registered with the Copyright Registry and the Screenwriters Association. A registration certificate acts as prima facie (first instance) evidence in a court of law, is proof of ownership and can be used as evidence in a court of law. 
 “Greater transparency can be encouraged through proper documentation and registration of scripts, maintaining clear records of drafts and their circulation, and developing clearer industry protocols for handling copyright complaints,” said Ketan Mukhija, partner and co-head, PE & VC, at Kochhar & Co, a law firm. “There should also be a balance between protecting genuine rights and ensuring due process, so that a film is not treated as infringing merely because an allegation has been made.”

docs.title: The Fed held steady on rates, leaving investors to sit tight, too
docs.text:
Global 
 The Fed held steady on rates, leaving investors to sit tight, too
 Sam Goldfarb , The Wall Street Journal 5 min read 29 Oct 2026, 06:59 AM IST 
 Summary
 Stocks and long-term bond yields edged higher after Wall Street read Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh as hesitant to hike aggressively. 
 Gift this article Check your portfolio 
 This is a Mint Premium article gifted to you.
Subscribe to enjoy similar stories.
 Subscribe now 
 The Federal Reserve is in a holding pattern. And so are markets.
 U.S. stocks and longer-term bond yields ticked higher after the Fed held interest rates steady as expected and Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh made comments that investors interpreted as slightly dovish—indicating that the central bank likely won’t embark on a rapid series of rate increases in the coming months.
 Warsh said at Wednesday’s postmeeting press conference that financial and credit conditions had tightened since the Fed raised rates last month—a sign, he suggested, that the central bank’s policies were already starting to work by moving toward “a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.”
 Stock investors were generally cheered by the tone of Warsh’s comments, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average ticking up 0.2%, or roughly 98 points, and the S&P 500 and Nasdaq composite both rising 0.3%. Bonds were more mixed, with longer-term yield rising even as short-term yields fell—a sign of some modest concern that the Fed might be too complacent in fighting inflation.
 “All in all, I would say the market is taking this as less likelihood of aggressive hiking,” said Anders Persson, chief investment officer and head of global fixed income at Nuveen. There was, he added, “nothing scary coming out of the conversation here today.”
 Heading into Wednesday, stocks had effectively treaded water in the six weeks since the Fed’s previous meeting, with the S&P 500 inching up 0.7% over that span. That broad performance, however, masked significant turmoil beneath the surface, as investors went hot and cold on the all-important AI trade, alternatively sapping and boosting demand for stocks in other sectors.
 Worries about rising borrowing costs and the future demand for AI models have dragged on tech shares for much of October. Still, many of them rebounded this week after Anthropic unveiled long-awaited paperwork for an initial public offering, showcasing data about its revenue growth, profitability and breadth of customers. The details helped reassure investors that demand for AI tools can keep pace with companies’ outsize spending on the infrastructure needed to power them.
 Results from tech giants Alphabet and Microsoft after the market close on Wednesday were expected to shed further light on those trends. Alphabet shares fell in after-hours trading after the Google parent reported advertising revenues that fell short of expectations. Microsoft rose in late trading after the software giant reported revenue that beat Wall Street estimates.
 Many investors see the Fed as one of the biggest threats to stocks right now. Expectations that the Fed will keep raising interest rates have driven up yields on U.S. government bonds. Higher yields have, in turn, put pressure on stocks by lifting borrowing costs across the economy and boosting the appeal of Treasurys as an alternative to riskier assets.
 Stocks and bonds now appear to be in an uneasy equilibrium. After the yield on the 10-year note reached a 24-year high above 5.3% earlier this month, investors quickly started selling tech stocks and buying bonds in a flight to safety. That pulled the 10-year yield back below 5%, providing some relief to stocks. But analysts say that yields could easily rise again if tech stocks continue to rebound and inflation remains elevated—a development that could eventually undermine that rally, as it did before.
 The 10-year yield was hovering just above 5% in late-afternoon trading Wednesday, according to Tradeweb, up from 4.992% Tuesday.
 Overall, the historic spending by tech companies is a major reason why the economy is proving so resilient and why the Fed is likely to raise rates further, said Jason Granet, chief investment officer at BNY.
 At some point, rising rates will slow the economy, but it could take time to get there because “there’s no one who’s calling for a massive ratchet-up in rates,” Granet said.
 Data to be released Thursday are expected to show that the core personal expenditures price index, a favored inflation gauge of the Fed, rose a little over 3% in September from a year earlier, well above the Fed’s 2% target.
 Some investors remain optimistic that inflation can gradually fall back to 2% without further rate increases, arguing that price increases are being driven by temporary factors such as President Trump’s tariff increases and rising energy costs spurred by the U.S.-Iran conflict.
 Some Fed officials have, in fact, framed last month’s rate increase as a risk-management move: a step to guard against inflation becoming entrenched rather than the first in a series of hikes. Others, though, have argued that rates need to move high enough to actively restrain the economy, raising the prospect of a more aggressive central bank that could cause more havoc in markets.
 Two officials cast dissenting votes Wednesday in favor of raising rates by a quarter of a percentage point. That was roughly in line with Wall Street’s expectations, though some were surprised that one of the dissenters was Fed governor Lisa Cook, who had never voted against a Fed decision in the past.
 As it stands, interest rate futures suggest that the investors see a roughly 85% chance that the Fed raises rates in December and a 57% chance of three more hikes in total by the end of next year, according to CME Group data.
 Oil prices remain near their highest levels of the year, making the Fed’s job more difficult as investors brace for a possible resumption of combat operations after next week’s U.S. midterm elec

docs.title: Top 10 equity mutual funds by foreign securities, REITs and InvITs holdings: WhiteOak Dividend Yield Fund tops list
docs.text:
According to a post by Value Research on X, “A handful of funds hold notable stakes in foreign securities, InvITs and REITs, assets that offer an alternative to the usual equity-debt mix. WhiteOak Capital Dividend Yield Fund leads, with nearly 80 per cent combined exposure, most of it in REITs. Technology funds such as Edelweiss Technology Fund and Franklin India Technology Fund, on the other hand, hold only foreign securities in this category.” Here's what you need to know about these equity mutual funds. *Source: Value Research, Only active funds are considered; September 2026 portfolio disclosures WhiteOak Capital Dividend Yield Fund, with 79.4% of net assets in REITs and InvITs, holds Bagmane Prime Office REIT, Nexus Select Trust, Mindspace Business Parks REIT and Knowledge Realty Trust. Its InvIT holdings include Cube Highways Fund, National Highways Infra Trust and Vertis Infrastructure Trust. Next on the list is Edelweiss Technology Fund, with 26.9% exposure to foreign securities. Its top holdings include Nvidia, Apple Inc. and Mphasis. Franklin India Technology Fund also invests exclusively in foreign securities with exposure of 20.2%. Franklin India Dividend Yield Fund, with 19.8% exposure to foreign securities and REITs, holds Taiwan-based MediaTek Inc and Embassy Office Parks REIT among its top holdings. WhiteOak Capital Multi Asset Allocation Fund, which has 19.6% exposure to foreign securities, InvITs, and REITs, counts Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, Cube Highways InvIT Fund, and Nexus Select Trust among its top holdings. Parag Parikh Flexi Cap Fund, with 18.2% exposure to foreign securities and REITs, has Alphabet and Embassy Office Parks REIT among its top holdings. For investors, these holdings offer exposure beyond domestic stocks and can diversify a portfolio across geographies and asset classes. Knowledge, courage, patience: Vijay Kedia's mantra for stock market success

 Ace market investor Vijay Kedia said stock market success rests on three pillars: knowledge, courage, and patience. In a conversation with Puneet Wadhwa at the Business Standard BFSI Insight Summit’s Smart Investor Arena, he also shared why long-term investing matters more than chasing quick returns. Edited excerpts:
 How has investing as a journey evolved across these years? 
 If you look at the ratio of traders versus investors, things have not changed much. Earlier too, the number of traders remained at 99 per cent, and the situation has not changed much as they are looking to make quick money. Most start with trading, but once they realise it's not an easy feat, they shift towards investing. If trading were so simple, everyone here would be a millionaire.
 Is it a game of skill or is it a game of luck? 
 Luck, of course, plays a very important role in the stock market because ultimately you are creating something from your mind. In the market, there is no guarantee; everything is backed by imagination and creativity. I consider it a form of art.
